title: Noah and the Flood
hook: In Genesis 8:1, we read something astonishing: "And God remembered Noah." The word "remembered" in Hebrew is *zakar*—not a casual recollection, but a covenantal awakening, the moment God moves to fulfill His promises. For five months Noah had floated in silence, the ark sealed with pitch, no windows to see out, no voice from heaven. Just the rocking of the waters and the smell of animals. Then God *remembered*. This same verb appears when God "remembered" Rachel, when He "remembered" His covenant with Abraham. It's the hinge of salvation history. These chapters are not primarily about a flood—they're about a God who never forgets His covenant people, even when the windows of heaven seem closed.
overview:
Genesis 6–11 spans from the wickedness preceding the Flood to the scattering at Babel, but Moses 8 in the Pearl of Great Price radically expands our understanding by revealing that Noah was not just a shipbuilder but a preacher of righteousness for 120 years. The Joseph Smith Translation restores over 150 verses to Genesis 6–9 alone, transforming the account from a simple divine judgment narrative into a story of prophetic warning, covenant-making, and the establishing of sacred ordinances. The narrative arc moves from universal corruption ("the earth was filled with violence") to divine sorrow ("it repented the Lord that he had made man"), to covenant preservation through one faithful family, to the establishment of the first explicit post-Fall covenant with humanity—complete with a sign, the rainbow, that endures to this day.

The central theological theme is divine justice held in tension with divine mercy. The Flood represents the most severe judgment in scripture, yet it's preceded by generations of prophetic pleading and followed immediately by covenant promises of preservation. Moses 8:17 tells us the Holy Ghost "ceased striving with them"—language that echoes Moroni's warnings and Nephi's prophecies about latter-day apostasy. This is not arbitrary divine wrath but the natural consequence of sustained rejection of light. The repeated phrase "Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord" (Genesis 6:8) introduces the Hebrew word *chen* (grace/favor), which will thread through the entire Old Testament as God's unmerited covenant loyalty.

Linguistically, Genesis 6 introduces vocabulary that becomes foundational: *nephilim* (often mistranslated "giants"), *racham* (the womb-deep compassion God feels), and the haunting phrase that humanity's "every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually." The Hebrew grammar intensifies: not just evil thoughts, but only evil, not just sometimes but continually. The ark itself (*tevah* in Hebrew) is a word used only twice in scripture—here and for the basket that saved baby Moses. Both are vessels of covenant preservation through waters of death. The dimensions of the ark (450 feet long, 75 feet wide, 45 feet high) have been shown by modern naval architects to produce the most stable design possible for a non-powered vessel—it couldn't sink even in a hurricane.

The Restoration transforms how we read these chapters. The JST reveals that Noah held the priesthood, preached repentance, and "called upon the children of men that they should repent" (Moses 8:16-24). The Book of Mormon prophet Alma quotes a "holy order" descending from Enoch through Noah (Alma 13:7-9), connecting Noah to Melchizedek and ultimately to Christ's priesthood. The temple endowment includes imagery of waters covering the earth and subsequent covenant-making with God, echoing the Flood narrative's structure of judgment, cleansing, emergence into a new world, and covenant with specific signs. Doctrine and Covenants 138:41 places Noah among those who "received their first lessons in the world of spirits" and were "prepared to perform their missions" before birth—Noah was foreordained.

These chapters connect to Christ through multiple threads. First Peter 3:18-21 explicitly links baptism to the Flood, calling the ark's salvation a "like figure" of baptismal deliverance through Christ. Noah becomes a "type" of Christ as the one righteous man through whom a new creation emerges. The covenant-making in Genesis 9 prefigures the "new and everlasting covenant" offered through Christ's atonement. The very structure of the ark narrative—descent into darkness, faithful waiting, emergence into light, covenant-making—mirrors the pattern of the atonement: death, burial, resurrection, eternal covenant. Even the dove that returns with an olive branch becomes in Christian tradition a symbol of the Holy Ghost bringing peace through Christ's completed work.
themes: Divine Grief and the Limits of Patience
The Rainbow Covenant and God's Promises

key_verses.text_kjv: But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord.
key_verses.insight: This is the first occurrence of the word "grace" (*chen*) in scripture. After six chapters of human failure, we finally encounter divine favor—not earned by Noah's perfection but granted as God's initiating covenant loyalty. The JST adds that Noah "found grace" because he was "a just man and perfect in his generation"—his righteousness was relational and covenantal, not absolute.

key_verses.text_kjv: And it repented Noah, and his heart was pained that the Lord had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at the heart.
key_verses.insight: The JST clarifies that it was Noah, not God, who felt grief—the Hebrew allows both readings, but Moses 8 shows Noah sharing in God's pain over human wickedness. This verse reveals the emotional cost of prophetic ministry: to see clearly what could have been, to plead for repentance, and to watch people choose destruction.

key_verses.text_kjv: And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged.
key_verses.insight: The Hebrew *zakar* (remembered) is a covenant term denoting action, not mere mental recall. When God "remembers," He moves to fulfill promises—here, to preserve the righteous remnant. The wind (*ruach*) is the same word as "spirit," echoing Genesis 1:2 where God's Spirit moved on the waters at creation. This is a re-creation moment.

key_verses.text_kjv: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
key_verses.insight: The rainbow is scripture's first covenant *sign*—a pattern that continues with circumcision, Sabbath, and sacrament. The Hebrew word for "bow" is the same as a warrior's bow; some scholars suggest God is setting aside His weapon of judgment and pointing it toward heaven, a divine promise never again to aim destruction at the earth through flood.

key_verses.text_kjv: And the Lord said, Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.
key_verses.insight: Unity without righteousness becomes dangerous. The Babel account shows that human consensus and technological achievement, divorced from covenant relationship with God, leads to pride and divine scattering. This verse has chilling modern applications about the power—and peril—of human unity when it's built on rebellion rather than revelation.

highlights.snippet_text: The Bible gives us two verses about Noah's righteousness. The JST restores 120 years of prophetic ministry. Moses 8 reveals Noah preached with power, calling humanity to repentance with the same urgency as Enoch before him. The Holy Ghost strove with that generation until it finally "ceased striving"—language Mormon uses about our day in Mormon 8:28. Noah wasn't just a carpenter; he was a rejected prophet.
highlights.label: Restoration

highlights.snippet_text: "My spirit shall not always strive with man" uses the Hebrew word *dun*, meaning to judge, contend, or govern. The image is of God's Spirit actively wrestling for the souls of humanity, not passively waiting. There comes a point—after Enoch, after Noah's preaching, after 120 years—when the divine wrestling stops. That withdrawal of the Spirit, not the flood waters, is the real judgment.
highlights.label: Hebrew

highlights.snippet_text: "The Lord shut him in" is one of scripture's most tender phrases. Noah didn't seal the ark himself—God did. This same Hebrew verb (*sagar*) appears in Isaiah 45:1 when God opens doors for Cyrus, and in Matthew 25 when the door shuts on the foolish virgins. Jesus later says "I am the door" (John 10:9). God alone controls the threshold between safety and judgment, and He personally sealed Noah inside.
highlights.label: Cross-Ref

highlights.snippet_text: "Gopher wood" appears nowhere else in scripture, and no one knows for certain what tree it refers to. Ancient Jewish tradition suggests cypress; others argue for resinous cedar. But the word *kopher* (the root of "gopher") means "atonement" or "covering"—the same root as *kaphar*, used for the mercy seat in the tabernacle. The ark's wood may be unknown, but its symbolic function as protective covering is crystal clear.
highlights.label: Historical

highlights.snippet_text: Ham's sin after the flood was serious enough to merit a prophetic curse on Canaan, his son. The Hebrew suggests more than accidental viewing—the phrase "saw the nakedness of his father" may indicate a violation or mockery. This troubling text was tragically misused to justify slavery, yet Moses 7:8,12 clarifies that Canaan's curse was about priesthood restriction in ancient times, not skin color or perpetual servitude. Context matters desperately.
highlights.label: Prophetic

highlights.snippet_text: The first thing Noah did after 371 days in the ark was build an altar. Not inventory his supplies, not plant crops, not assess the damage. He worshiped. After trauma, after loss, after watching the world drown, his first act was covenant gratitude. For modern members emerging from their own trials—illness, divorce, loss—this sets the pattern: we rebuild altars before we rebuild houses.
highlights.label: Application

restoration_lens:
The Joseph Smith Translation transforms the flood narrative from a story about God's wrath into a story about prophetic warning and covenant preparation. Moses 8:16-30 adds entire discourses of Noah preaching repentance, being rejected, and warning of coming judgment—material completely absent from Genesis. The JST reveals that Noah was ordained to the priesthood at age ten (Moses 8:12, footnote), that he 'walked with God' just as Enoch did (using the same Hebrew phrase for intimate fellowship), and that he labored for generations calling people to enter the ark of safety. This changes everything. The flood wasn't a surprise; it was the culmination of a centuries-long prophetic warning. When we read Moses 8:20—'the Gospel began to be preached, from the beginning'—we realize Noah stood in a direct line of priesthood authority from Adam through Seth through Enoch, holding the same Melchizedek Priesthood that would later be conferred on Abraham. Alma 13:7-9 places Noah explicitly in the 'holy order of God,' connecting flood-era covenant-making to temple ordinances.

The Book of Mormon prophets consistently invoke Noah as a type of covenant warning. Alma tells the people of Ammonihah that 'as the Lord liveth, as many of the Lamanites as believed in their preaching, and were converted unto the Lord, never did fall away... but as many as would not hear his words, were destroyed'—the same pattern as Noah's generation (Alma 23:6). Moroni warns latter-day readers that 'the Holy Ghost... ceased striving with them' (Mormon 8:28), using language identical to Moses 8:17. Ether 2:10 declares that any nation on the promised land that ripens in iniquity faces destruction 'as the Lord did the Jaredites'—who themselves predated Noah but experienced similar divine limits to patience. The entire Nephite prophetic tradition sees the Flood as the template for understanding God's justice: long-suffering patience, clear warning through prophets, an ark of covenant safety, and eventual judgment on those who refuse.

Doctrine and Covenants 84:14-15 traces priesthood lineage directly through Noah, and D&C 138:41 reveals that Noah was among the noble and great ones, 'chosen before they were born' and instructed 'even before they were born' regarding their earthly missions. Modern prophets have connected flood imagery to baptism (as Peter did in 1 Peter 3:21) and to temple covenants. President Russell M. Nelson taught that temple covenants are our 'ark of safety' in turbulent times. The rainbow covenant of Genesis 9, with its explicit promise that 'the waters shall no more become a flood to destroy all flesh,' becomes in Restoration theology a type of God's covenant faithfulness—once He makes covenant promises, marked by signs, He keeps them eternally. The sacrament prayers echo this: 'always remember him and keep his commandments'—the same pattern of remembering established at Noah's altar in Genesis 8:20-21.
application:
For covenant members today, these chapters pose urgent questions about recognizing prophetic warning before judgment arrives. Noah preached for 120 years; people saw the ark being built for decades. Wickedness didn't arrive suddenly—it ripened over generations until 'every imagination of the thoughts of [their] hearts was only evil continually.' The modern application cuts deep: Can we recognize the slow drift toward spiritual danger in our own lives, families, and communities before the windows of heaven close? Moses 8:17's warning that the Spirit will 'cease striving' suggests there is a limit to divine patience, not because God stops loving us, but because sustained rejection of light eventually hardens hearts beyond the reach of the Spirit. For members navigating a secular culture that mocks covenant living, Noah's experience validates the loneliness of standing firm when everyone else considers you foolish. Building an ark in the desert looked insane—until it rained.

The flood narrative also provides profound comfort about God's covenant memory. Genesis 8:1—'God remembered Noah'—becomes a lifeline for anyone who feels forgotten during long trials. Like Noah sealed in the ark with no windows, no voice from heaven, just months of dark floating and waiting, covenant members sometimes experience seasons when heaven seems silent, when prayers feel unanswered, when we're simply enduring in faith. But God's 'remembering' is not forgetfulness corrected; it's covenant faithfulness enacted. He remembered Rachel and opened her womb; He remembered Israel in Egypt and sent Moses; He remembered Hannah and gave her Samuel. To be 'remembered' by God means He's moving to fulfill His promises to you, even when you can't yet see it. The ark is still floating; the dove will return; the ground will appear. For members enduring infertility, chronic illness, wayward children, or years of feeling spiritually adrift, Noah's story says: God has not forgotten you. He is keeping count of the days. His covenant memory is perfect.

Finally, Genesis 8:20's image of Noah building an altar immediately upon leaving the ark reshapes how we approach life after trauma or trial. Before assessing damage, before rebuilding routines, before making plans—worship. Gratitude precedes reconstruction. For returned missionaries struggling to reintegrate, for couples emerging from marriage crises, for anyone stepping into a 'new world' after the floodwaters of their own trials recede, the pattern is clear: rebuild your altar first. Renew covenants. Offer sacrifice (time, heart, will) to God. Only then does He promise 'seedtime and harvest... shall not cease' (Genesis 8:22). The rainbow covenant reminds us that God makes promises and keeps them—His covenant signs are visible in the sky after every storm. The sacrament table is our weekly rainbow, our sign that God remembers His covenant with us and will never forget.
